content: Human language comprehension occurs when an individual processes a linguistic utterance, whether it is presented in isolation or within the context of a conversation or text. Numerous studies on human language comprehension have concentrated on the reading of single sentences without any contextual information. However, extensive research has demonstrated that language comprehension is influenced not only by the immediate context preceding a given utterance but also by various other factors. Ambiguity and Sentence Comprehension Research Sentence comprehension must address ambiguities in spoken and written language, including lexical, structural, and semantic ambiguities. Ambiguity is pervasive, yet humans typically resolve it so effortlessly that they are often unaware of its presence. For instance, the sentence Time flies like an arrow can be interpreted in at least three ways: (1) time moves as quickly as an arrow, (2) a special type of fly called time fly likes arrows, or (3) measure the speed of flies in the same way you would measure the speed of an arrow. Typically, readers are only conscious of the first interpretation. Ambiguities can be classified as either local or global. A sentence is globally ambiguous if it has two distinct interpretations. For example, in the sentence Someone shot the servant of the actress who was on the balcony, it is unclear whether the servant or the actress was on the balcony. Similarly, in The cop chased the criminal with a fast car, it is ambiguous whether the cop or the criminal had the fast car. While comprehenders may have a preferred interpretation in such cases, syntactically and semantically, neither interpretation can be definitively ruled out. Local ambiguities, on the other hand, are temporary and persist only for a short duration as the utterance is being processed. These ambiguities are resolved as the sentence unfolds, resulting in a single interpretation for the complete utterance. For example, in the sentence The critic wrote the interview was enlightening, ambiguity arises when the phrase The critic wrote the book is encountered, but the ambiguity is resolved upon processing was enlightening, which clarifies that the critic wrote about the book rather than being its author. When readers process local ambiguities, they immediately settle on one possible interpretation without waiting for additional information to clarify the ambiguity. This behavior is known as incremental processing. If the sentence takes an unexpected turn, processing slows down, as evidenced by increased reading times. Local ambiguities have been used as test cases to investigate the influence of various factors on human sentence processing. If a factor helps readers avoid difficulty, it is evident that this factor plays a role in sentence comprehension. Theories about Language Comprehension Experimental research has led to the development of numerous hypotheses regarding the architecture and mechanisms underlying sentence comprehension. Key theoretical debates in the field include modularity versus interactive processing and serial versus parallel computation of analyses. Architectural Issues 1. Modular vs. Interactive Processing A modular view of sentence processing posits that each factor involved in comprehension operates within its own module, with limited communication between modules. For example, syntactic analysis occurs independently of semantic analysis or context-dependent information, which are processed separately. Modular accounts often assume a feed-forward architecture, where the output of one processing step is passed to the next without feedback mechanisms to correct earlier outputs. Syntactic processing is typically considered the foundational step, feeding into semantic processing and the integration of other information. In contrast, interactive accounts propose that all available information is processed simultaneously and can immediately influence the computation of the final analysis. 2. Serial vs. Parallel Processing Serial accounts suggest that humans initially construct only one possible interpretation of a sentence and attempt another interpretation only if the first one proves incorrect. Parallel accounts, on the other hand, propose that multiple interpretations are constructed simultaneously. To explain why comprehenders are usually aware of only one interpretation, models may assume that all analyses are ranked, with the highest-ranking interpretation being entertained. Models of Sentence Processing 1. Garden Path Model The Garden Path Model is a serial, modular parsing model. It suggests that a single syntactic parse is initially constructed by a syntactic module. Contextual and semantic factors influence processing at a later stage and can trigger re-analysis of the syntactic parse. Re-analysis is cognitively costly and results in observable slowdowns in reading. When the parser encounters ambiguity, it follows two principles: Late Closure: New words or phrases are attached to the current clause. Minimal Attachment: The parser constructs the simplest syntactic structure possible, with the fewest phrasal nodes. While the Garden Path Model has been influential, it is no longer a standard explanation for human sentence processing due to its strictly serial architecture. Most contemporary models assume some degree of early interaction between different factors. Additionally, its parsing principles, such as Minimal Attachment, have been criticized for their reliance on specific syntactic representations. Nevertheless, the Garden Path Model has significantly shaped the field. 2. Constraint-Based Model The Constraint-Based Model is parallel and interactive. It posits that multiple syntactic analyses are generated simultaneously, guided by various constraints such as lexical knowledge, context, and prior experience. Evidence supporting this model includes findings that comprehenders use their lexical knowledge during sentence processing. For example, garden path sentences like The florist sent the flowers was very pleased challenge the Garden Path Model but align with the Constraint-Based Model, as comprehenders rely on lexical and contextual cues to resolve ambiguity. Findings in Sentence Comprehension 1. Lexical Preferences Lexical meaning influences sentence comprehension. For instance, the garden path sentence She saw her duck and some eggs initially leads readers to think of duck eggs, whereas She saw her duck and fall down prompts a different interpretation. The latter sentence requires more processing time because it involves constructing two verb phrases (VPs). 2. Incomplete or Inaccurate Representations Christianson et al. (2001) investigated whether structural representations of sentences are complete and accurate during parsing. For example, in the sentence While Anna dressed the baby played in the crib, readers often correctly answer that the baby played in the crib but make errors when asked if Anna dressed the baby. Ferreira (2003) found that readers do not immediately construct complete and accurate representations of sentences. Active sentences yield 100% accuracy, while passive sentences (e.g., The man was bitten by the dog vs. The dog was bitten by the man) result in 75% accuracy. These studies highlight the role of expectations in sentence comprehension.
